q: Does the proven prefactor advantage of Nakaji-FAE over Grinko-IQAE (4.1e3 vs 1.15e6, ~280x) survive a head-to-head empirical race on identical (a, epsilon) targets, and does the empirical prefactor gap track the ratio of proven bounds or collapse in practice?
basis: Our replication only sanity-checked FAE's own empirical prefactor against its own upper bound; we did NOT implement Grinko IQAE and race the two on matched amplitudes. This is the single most publishable single-number comparison in the paper and the largest gap in the current replication (see Critique item 1).
next_steps: Implement Grinko IQAE (arXiv:1912.05559) as a third algorithm in code/iqae.py, reusing the existing oracle.py Grover operator; run the same experiment.py sweep for a in {0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4} at matched N_orac budgets, extract per-a prefactors from the log10(N_orac) = 1*log10(1/eps) + log10(C) fits (forced Heisenberg slope), and report the empirical FAE-to-IQAE prefactor ratio alongside the proven-bound ratio; if the empirical ratio is <<280, quantify the effective advantage.

q: Does FAE's two-stage design retain its edge over both IQAE and MLAE under realistic depolarising and readout noise, or does the Chernoff-derived shot count (N_shot^1st = 1944*ln(2/delta_c)) get eaten by noise-induced bias in cos(2(2^k+1)theta) estimates?
basis: Everything in this replication is noiseless statevector (Critique item 3). FAE's marketing pitch is NISQ-friendliness (no deep controlled-Q), so its behavior under realistic noise IS the point --- and we did not test it. A biased cosine estimate would bleed into arccos in stage 1 and into the trig-addition in stage 2; the failure mode is not obvious.
next_steps: Wrap oracle.py's exact_prob_good_after_Qm with a depolarising channel p_depol in {1e-4, 1e-3, 1e-2} per Q^m application (composition of ~4m gate errors per m) and a readout confusion matrix (p_01, p_10) in {0, 0.01, 0.03}; rerun FAE, IQAE, and MLAE at a=0.3 across the noise grid; report which algorithm's slope stays closest to 1 and at what noise level FAE loses its rigorous-guarantee regime (i.e., where the Chernoff bound becomes vacuous).

q: Can a noise-adaptive query schedule (increase N_shot per round when the observed cosine variance exceeds the Chernoff-implied variance) recover FAE's Heisenberg scaling under noise more efficiently than fixed conservative shot counts?
basis: FAE's N_shot^1st = 1944*ln(2/delta_c) is set to satisfy the worst-case Chernoff bound (Critique item 2 in ~10,300 shots at delta_c=0.01). Under noise, either this is under-shot (biased) or over-shot (wasted queries). An adaptive schedule that inflates N_shot when the observed cos variance is above Chernoff would trade rigor for query economy.
next_steps: Implement fae_adaptive.py: after each COS(m, N_shot_min=100) call, compute the empirical variance of c_m across a small pilot batch, compare to the Chernoff-implied variance 1/(2*N_shot_min), and if the pilot variance is >2x expected, double N_shot until the ratio is <=2; measure N_orac(eps) under the same noise grid as the previous question and compare to fixed-shot FAE. Report the query-economy ratio at eps=1e-3.

q: Does replacing FAE's iteration schedule m_k = 2^k with an ML-selected schedule (a small policy network trained to pick the next m_k given the current [theta_min, theta_max] and shot budget) reduce the per-a prefactor C without breaking the Heisenberg 1/epsilon scaling?
basis: The 2^k doubling schedule is a natural, algorithm-agnostic default (also used by IQAE and MLAE), but nothing forces it to be optimal for a given a. Since our fit gives per-a prefactors C in {88.9 (a=0.3), similar for others}, there is head-room if the schedule can adapt to interval width. Candidate probe explicitly suggested by Rick.
next_steps: Frame schedule selection as a small MDP: state = (theta_min, theta_max, k, remaining N_orac budget), action = m_{k+1} in a bounded set, reward = -log(final |a_hat - a|); train a policy on offline traces from the existing sweep_raw.csv via behavior cloning + REINFORCE with a KL penalty to the 2^k baseline; evaluate on held-out a values and report the median N_orac reduction at fixed eps.

q: Does FAE deliver a measurable end-to-end speedup for a canonical quant-finance application (European call option pricing via QAE, as in Woerner-Egger 2019 arXiv:1806.06893) at commercially interesting error targets (eps in [1e-3, 1e-4]), and is the constant-factor advantage over IQAE preserved once the payoff-loading circuit is included in the query count?
basis: AE's most-cited application is quant-finance Monte-Carlo replacement; the paper positions FAE as the NISQ-friendly successor. If the payoff-loading oracle A_payoff dominates the query count (which is common for realistic loss distributions), FAE's constant-factor win on the Q-application count may or may not translate to end-to-end wallclock. Candidate probe explicitly suggested by Rick.
next_steps: Reuse Qiskit-Finance's EuropeanCallPricing (or reimplement its A_load and payoff comparator as a standalone module) as the A oracle in oracle.py; run FAE, IQAE, and canonical QPE-QAE (small-qubit) at eps in {1e-2, 1e-3} for strike-price grids typical of Woerner-Egger; report total oracle calls (loading + Q) per eps and end-to-end call-price RMSE. Flag whether FAE's advantage over IQAE at the algorithm level survives the loading-cost dilution.
